term_glossary.tooltip: A DC distribution domain below medium-voltage class; in this course the SST output interface is unipolar 800 VDC.
Resistive heating proportional to the square of current times resistance. Lower current can sharply reduce loss for the same conductor resistance.
Equipment and controls that store energy and later supply electrical power for ride-through, backup, smoothing, or other defined services.
A megawatt-scale power-electronic converter that accepts MVAC and produces regulated LVDC through switched conversion and isolation.
A product framework that defines interfaces and observable behavior while allowing suppliers freedom in internal implementation.
Galvanic separation implemented through a transformer operating above line frequency, enabling smaller magnetics while adding switching and insulation challenges.
An intermediate DC energy node, often using capacitance, between converter stages.
Separation that prevents a direct conductive path while allowing energy transfer through a transformer or other isolation mechanism.
A semiconductor material class, including silicon carbide and gallium nitride, that can support high-voltage and high-frequency power switching.
Medium-frequency transformer or high-frequency transformer used for voltage transformation and isolation in switched converters.
A requirement-bearing part of a specification. Non-normative material provides context or examples without mandating an implementation.
An insulation-withstand rating for standardized high-voltage impulse conditions.
How quickly system frequency changes, expressed here in hertz per second.
A grounding method that limits ground-fault current through intentional resistance while enabling fault detection and controlled response.
An enclosure rating intended to provide a degree of protection for outdoor equipment against rain, sleet, and external ice formation.
The organization or official responsible for interpreting and enforcing applicable codes and approvals.
To be determined. A draft entry that remains open and must not be treated as a finalized requirement.
A grounded-neutral method using resistance to limit fault current while retaining detectable ground-fault behavior.
A normalized quantity expressed relative to nominal voltage; 1.0 per unit equals the nominal value.
The required behavior during a temporary input-voltage reduction, including current limits and coordinated ESS support.
The duration and behavior required while input frequency is outside the normal continuous band.
Controlled charging of DC-link capacitance before the main power path is fully enabled, limiting inrush and verifying readiness.
An architecture with N capacity required for load plus C additional capacity or blocks available for redundancy.
Continuous monitoring used to detect declining insulation resistance or a first ground fault in an unearthed or impedance-grounded DC system.
Coordination that isolates the smallest practical faulted section while allowing unaffected parts of the system to continue operating.
A coordinated medium-voltage power-conversion and energy-storage system capable of supplying critical output during upstream interruption.
An energy-storage architecture connected to a DC bus, sharing or coordinating DC conversion and protection interfaces.

bullets.text: Supports high-voltage, efficient switching and is central to current SST development.
Has emerging potential, but application maturity and voltage class must match the product.

slides.title: Programmability and Modularity Expand the Trade Space

slides.title: What Makes an SST Different
items: Switched conversion integrates isolation, regulation, sensing, and control into an active product.

WBG devices and higher-frequency magnetics create power-density opportunity with new engineering risks.
Capabilities such as programmability and modularity must be proven through system-level validation.

slides.title: Grounding Begins Upstream of the SST

bullets.text: A Wye secondary establishes a neutral reference on the supplying system.
The specification lists low-resistance grounding or solid grounding.
Fault current, protection sensitivity, transient voltage, and insulation coordination depend on the actual grounding design.

figure.alt: Simplified Wye-secondary grounding diagram feeding the three-phase SST input with protective earth.
figure.caption: Grounding must be coordinated with the source transformer, site protection study, and product insulation design.

entries.text: Three phase, three wire + protective earth
Protection sees the actual source and neutral treatment
Coordinate cable, surge, insulation, and fault studies

slides.title: The DC Load Sees a Coordinated SST–ESS Response

figure.alt: Silent animation showing a grid-voltage sag, current-limited SST input, zero-input severe sag, and ESS power filling the DC output requirement.
figure.caption: The SST and ESS coordinate so the 800 VDC output remains supported across the specified voltage regions.

entries.text: ACCEPTABLE. SST supplies output. ESS idle / charging. Output remains supported · acceptable voltage/frequency return enables immediate recovery
LVRT RANGE 1. SST current ≤ nominal. ESS fills shortfall
LVRT RANGE 2. SST input current = 0. ESS supplies 100%

slides.title: Ride Through First, Then Recover Without a Second Event

bullets.text: 57.0–<58.8 Hz and >61.2–61.8 Hz for 299 seconds.
Below 57 Hz or above 61.8 Hz, the SST may ride through or trip.
ESS recharge adds load and must respect source and utility ramp limits.

figure.alt: Frequency ride-through bar showing continuous, 299-second, and may-trip operating regions.
figure.caption: OCP SST v0.3 frequency ride-through bands, centered on a 60 Hz system.

slides.title: Six States Make Behavior Observable

figure.alt: State model showing OFF, Standby, Precharged, ON, FAULT, and WARNING with normal and abnormal transition paths.
figure.caption: State labels from OCP SST v0.3: S0, Sb, Sp, S1, S2, and S3.

slides.title: State, Energy Source, and Alarm Severity Are Different Axes

bullets.text: Standby → precharge → ON after permissives and controlled DC-link energization.
An abnormal condition is reported while continued operation may remain possible.
Protection moves the unit to FAULT and invokes the defined recovery or service path.
Grid and ESS contribution can change without a state transition when quality returns promptly.

figure.alt: Parallel sequence lanes for normal startup, warning escalation, fault shutdown, and ride-through recovery.
figure.caption: Use one coordinated control narrative for power source, state, alarm, and recovery behavior.

entries.text: Sb Standby › Sp Precharged › S1 ON
S1 remains ON · SST input changes · ESS fills output · immediate recovery
S3 reports abnormal condition · operation may continue · investigate
S2 protective response · isolate cause · follow defined recovery path

slides.title: An SST Is a Controlled Grid Participant
items: Upstream grounding establishes the fault-current and insulation environment at the MVAC interface.
LVRT range 1 limits SST input current; range 2 uses zero SST input current while ESS supports output.
58.8–61.2 Hz is continuous; adjacent bands require 299 seconds; outer bands may trip.
ESS recharge is additive site load and belongs in the post-event control strategy.
Six operating states make normal, warning, fault, startup, and recovery behavior deterministic.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Ride-through can recover without a state transition; precharge, warning, and controlled recharge remain distinct concepts.

slides.title: Deploy the System, Not Just the Converter
items: Appendix A redundancy patterns are useful design context but explicitly non-normative.
Grounding, insulation monitoring, converter limits, and protection timing form one coordination problem.
Capacitance, SST controls, ESS discharge, backup, grid services, and recharge occupy different timescales.
ESS placement changes fault, charging, maintenance, fire-protection, controls, and approval boundaries.
A v0.3 deployment plan must combine product tests, system validation, pilot evidence, and community feedback.

questions.prompt: How should the Appendix A redundancy diagrams be used?

choices.text: As non-normative application examples that prompt system-level design questions
As mandatory one-line designs for every SST deployment
choices.feedback_incorrect: Appendix A labels the figures non-normative.

choices.text: As a replacement for protection and capacity studies
choices.feedback_incorrect: The examples do not establish site-specific ratings, timing, or selectivity.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The diagrams are application context, not mandatory designs.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the normative product boundary versus Appendix A context.

questions.prompt: Which items belong in system-level SST and ESS validation?

choices.text: Grounding, insulation monitoring, and selective protection
ESS discharge response and controlled recharge
Communications, states, alarms, and auxiliary-power behavior
Only the SST nameplate voltage

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Deployment validation spans electrical, storage, controls, protection, and operational boundaries.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A nameplate is necessary but cannot prove coordinated system behavior.
